local_calendar.t: State law has every Colorado county except the two that are cities and counties, Denver and Broomfield, elect a clerk and recorder, treasurer, assessor, sheriff, coroner and surveyor on November 3, 2026, along with the county commissioners whose four-year terms are up; voters of the Regional Transportation District elect directors in seven of its fifteen director districts; and judges of the district courts, the county courts and Denver's juvenile and probate courts face a yes or no retention vote. School boards are elected in November of odd-numbered years and special district boards in May of odd-numbered years; towns regularly vote in April of even-numbered years and cities in November of odd-numbered years, unless a municipality's voters have moved its election to November of even-numbered years, in which case it shares this ballot. No district attorney is on the Secretary of State's 2026 list.

measures.t: Law Enforcement Communication with Federal Immigration Authorities
measures.q: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution requiring law enforcement to notify the department of homeland security when a person is charged with either a violent crime or any crime if the person has a prior felony conviction if law enforcement cannot determine that the person is lawfully present in the United States?
measures.s:
Amendment 81 proposes amending the Colorado Constitution to:
require state and local law enforcement to make a reasonable effort to determine whether an individual charged with a crime is lawfully present, if the charge is a crime of violence or the individual has a prior felony conviction; and
notify federal immigration authorities within 72 hours of filing charges if law enforcement cannot determine that the charged individual is lawfully present in the United States.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Amendment 81 requires law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities after filing certain criminal charges against individuals who are not confirmed to be lawfully present.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Amendment 81 maintains current law, which allows cooperation with federal immigration authorities in some criminal matters, but limits state and local law enforcement involvement in civil immigration enforcement.
measures.f:
State Spending
In state budget year 2026-27, state spending and workload will increase for agencies that employ law enforcement officers. Two departments require system updates: the Department of Revenue requires $50,000 to access federal databases and make programming changes, and the Department of Natural Resources requires $10,000 to update computer systems. The measure does not specify a funding source to pay for these costs and it is assumed that they will be paid from the General Fund. Workload may also increase in these departments, as well as the departments of Higher Education, Human Services, Judicial, Law, and Public Safety, to the extent they are required to determine a charged individual's immigration status and communicate with the federal government on affected cases; however, this work will be primarily conducted by local governments.
Local Government Spending
Local law enforcement agencies, including police, district attorney offices, and Regional Transportation District officers, will have increased workload and potential spending. As with the state, the added workload involves determining a charged individual's immigration status and communicating with the federal government on affected cases. Because this determination happens after charges are filed, most of the workload will fall on district attorney offices. The amount of work will vary by jurisdiction depending on how many individuals are charged there. Spending, if incurred, will be on systems updates.

measures.t: Constitutional Right to Purchase and Sell Natural Gas
measures.q: Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating new law granting the right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses and for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas to consumers?
measures.s:
Amendment 82 proposes amending the Colorado Constitution to:
establish a constitutional right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating; and
establish a constitutional right for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas for use in homes and businesses.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Amendment 82 establishes a state constitutional right to purchase and sell natural gas for use in homes and businesses.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Amendment 82 maintains current law and regulations related to the purchase and sale of natural gas.
measures.f:
State Spending
The measure may minimally increase expenditures for state agencies, primarily the Department of Local Affairs, to revise technical assistance to local governments concerning building codes that conflict with the right to purchase or sell natural gas. The measure may also increase workload and legal services for state agencies that regulate or monitor emissions from natural gas utilities or intervene in those cases, including the Public Utilities Commission, the Department of Natural Resources, the Department of Public Health and Environment, and the Colorado Energy Office.
Local Government Spending
Local governments that currently have or are considering building codes that regulate, prohibit or restrict natural gas in commercial and residential development may have increased legal services and costs to conform the codes with state law, and to modify permitting, inspection, and compliance activities.

require voters to provide identification information, in addition to their signature, for their mail ballots to be counted.

measures.f:
The measure will increase state and local spending by up to $2.7 million in the initial budget year 2026-27, and $1.2 million annually in future years for voter outreach, printing, and election staff to verify voter information. These costs will be divided between state and local governments as discussed below.
Local Government Spending
The new verification process under the measure will increase county spending by up to $2.5 million in the 2026-27 budget year and up to $1.2 million in future years. About 45 percent of these county costs will be reimbursed by the state government. These costs are driven from several new requirements under the measure. First, election judges must review identification numbers provided by voters, which will increase staffing hours and overtime during elections. Second, county election offices must notify voters of any discrepancies involving their identification information, which will require sending a postcard or digital notification to voters and segregating ballots until valid identification is provided. Lastly, county election offices will also be required to update ballot materials and envelopes, modify various elections systems, and conduct voter outreach.
State Spending
The Department of State will have increased costs to inform voters of the changes to mail voting across the state and to reimburse counties. Specifically, the department will need to conduct an outreach and communication campaign at a cost of $100,000 in state budget year 2026-27 and $200,000 in state budget year 2027-28. The department will also have ongoing workload and costs for outreach and printed materials estimated at $20,000 for each presidential primary, statewide primary, and general election. As discussed above, the state will also have costs to reimburse counties for a portion of their costs under the measure. This reimbursement is estimated to be up to $1.1 million in during the 2026-27 budget year, and up to $500,000 for in future years. Historically, these costs have been paid using fees and other revenue collected by the department, rather than from the state General Fund.
State Revenue
To cover the costs in the Department of State discussed above, business filing fees may need to be raised to cover all or some of the costs of this measure. The fees affected, the timing of any increase, and the actual amount of fee charges will be set administratively by the department based on its available fund balance and total program costs.

measures.t: Graduated Income Tax
measures.q: SHALL STATE TAXES BE INCREASED $2.7 BILLION ANNUALLY, IN ORDER TO INCREASE OR IMPROVE LEVELS OF PUBLIC SERVICES, INCLUDING K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION SERVICES, BY AN AMENDMENT TO THE COLORADO CONSTITUTION AND A CHANGE TO THE COLORADO REVISED STATUTES REPEALING EXISTING LAW AND CREATING NEW LAW TO REPLACE THE UNIFORM STATE INCOME TAX RATE WITH A GRADUATED INCOME TAX STRUCTURE, AND, IN CONNECTION THEREWITH, AMENDING THE TAXPAYER’S BILL OF RIGHTS TO ELIMINATE THE CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENT FOR ALL TAXABLE NET INCOME TO BE TAXED AT ONE RATE WITH NO ADDED TAX ON INCOME; ESTABLISHING VARIOUS INCOME TAX RATES BASED ON THE AMOUNT OF TAXABLE INCOME EARNED BY INDIVIDUALS, ESTATES, TRUSTS, AND CORPORATIONS, WHILE MAINTAINING THE CURRENT 4.4% TAX ON INCOME FROM THE SALE OF A PRINCIPAL RESIDENCE, WHICH WILL RESULT IN THE ESTIMATED CHANGE IN INCOME TAXES OWED BY INDIVIDUALS AS IDENTIFIED IN THE FOLLOWING TABLE; AND AUTHORIZING THE STATE TO RETAIN AND SPEND ANY INCREASED REVENUE FROM THE NEW TAX STRUCTURE, AS A VOTER-APPROVED REVENUE CHANGE, TO SUPPLEMENT CURRENT LEVELS OF FUNDING FOR K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION PROGRAMS?
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Amendment 87 creates a graduated state income tax that increases revenue; uses the additional money for K-12 education, health care, and early childhood care and education; and exempts additional revenue collected from the state’s constitutional revenue limit.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Amendment 87 keeps the current constitutional requirement for a flat state income tax rate.
measures.f:
Taxpayer Impacts
Amendment 87 will decrease the amount of income tax owed by taxpayers with Colorado taxable income of less than $510,834 and increase the amount of income tax owed by taxpayers with Colorado taxable income of $510,834 and above. State law requires Legislative Council Staff to estimate the potential tax burden on affected taxpayers within specified federal adjusted gross income categories. Federal adjusted gross income is total income from all sources, with certain adjustments, as determined when filing federal income taxes. Colorado taxable income, calculated when filing state income taxes, is based on federal adjusted gross income with additional adjustments required or allowed under state law. Table 3 shows the expected change in tax burden by federal adjusted gross income category. The measure has no impact on current TABOR refunds or TABOR refund mechanisms.
State Revenue
By replacing the state flat income tax with a graduated income tax, the measure increases revenue from income taxes by an estimated $958.4 million in budget year 2026-27, $1.972 billion in budget year 2027-28, and increasing amounts in future years based on income and population growth. The estimate for budget year 2026-27 represents a half-year impact for tax year 2027. The additional revenue will be credited to the Colorado Future’s Account created in the measure. The increased revenue is exempt from TABOR as a voter-approved revenue change. The state budget year begins each July 1 and ends on June 30.
State law requires Legislative Council Staff to include an estimate of the maximum dollar amount of the change in state government revenue for the first full fiscal year of a proposed tax increase. This is the number that appears in the ballot question. The estimates in the previous paragraph represent the revenue impact of the measure under the current Legislative Council Staff revenue forecast. Based on forecast error that could occur, the maximum dollar amount of the change in state government revenue and fiscal year spending for budget year 2027-28 is estimated as an increase of $2.7 billion.
State Spending
The measure increases the amount of state revenue available to spend for the purposes identified in the measure, including K-12 education, health care, and early childhood care and education, in FY 2026-27 and future fiscal years. To administer the tax rate change, the measure is expected to increase one-time spending in the Department of Revenue by $98,000.
School District Revenue and Spending
The measure increases available state funding to school districts. The exact amount distributed to school districts will depend on decisions made by the General Assembly when allocating money from the Colorado Future’s Account.
State Spending and Tax Increases
Article X, Section 20, of the Colorado Constitution requires that the following fiscal information be provided when a tax increase question is on the ballot:
estimates or actual amounts of state fiscal year spending for the current year and each of the past four years with the overall percentage and dollar change; and
for the first full year of the proposed tax increase, estimates of the maximum dollar amount of the tax increase and of fiscal year spending without the increase.
“Fiscal year spending” is a legal term in the Colorado Constitution. It equals the amount of revenue subject to the constitutional spending limit that the state or a district is permitted to keep and either spend or save for a single year. Table 4 shows state fiscal year spending for the current year and each of the past four years.

measures.s:
Proposition NN proposes amending the Colorado statutes to
allow the state to keep some or all of the revenue that the state's constitutional revenue limit, also known as the Taxpayer's Bill of Rights (TABOR), would otherwise require to be refunded to taxpayers, up to the amount the state spends on public education; and
spend the retained revenue to increase funding for K-12 education and programs that support children, and, after ten years, K-12 education and any other purposes to be determined by the state legislature.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Proposition NN allows the state to keep some or all of the revenue that otherwise would be refunded to taxpayers under TABOR. The retained revenue must be spent on K-12 education, programs that support children, and any other purposes.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Proposition NN maintains current TABOR refunds and funding levels for K-12 education, programs that support children, and other state purposes.
measures.f:
Taxpayer Impacts
Proposition NN is expected to reduce the amount refunded to taxpayers by $329.9 million in the current 2026-27 budget year, $521.0 million in the 2027-28 budget year, and by varying amounts in future years. This eliminates TABOR refunds for budget years 2026-27 and 2027-28. Table 1 shows estimated TABOR refunds under Proposition NN for certain income levels.
A forecast of state revenue subject to TABOR is not available beyond budget year 2027-28. The impact of Proposition NN on TABOR refunds will vary significantly across different years, such that it could have no impact on TABOR refunds in some years and reduce them by over $1,000 per taxpayer in other years. The actual amount that the measure reduces TABOR refunds will depend on how much money the state collects above the current TABOR limit in future years.
State Spending
The measure increases state spending by an estimated $329.9 million in budget year 2026-27 and $521.0 million in budget year 2027-28 on net, and by varying amounts in future years. Changes in state spending are shown in Table 2.
As shown in Table 2, $153.1 million that would be available for the general state budget under current law is instead deposited in the Children’s Account for budget years 2026-27 and 2027-28 only. This reduces General Fund spending in each of these two years.
Long‑term spending. After ten years, there is no longer a requirement for half of the money in the account to be spent on K-12 education and half on children’s programs. Beginning in the 2036-37 budget year, the measure increases state spending for property tax reimbursements and funding for teacher pay and retention, smaller class sizes, and career and technical education. Any remaining funds may be used for any purposes as determined by the state legislature.
School Districts
Proposition NN increases state funding for school districts by an estimated $241.5 million in budget year 2026-27 and $234.0 million in budget year 2027-28. Funding for teacher pay and retention, smaller class sizes, and career and technical education will be distributed based on each school district’s percentage of statewide school finance funding under the state’s new school finance formula. Funding for school services, disability services, and increasing annual instructional hours will be distributed in a manner determined by the state legislature.

measures.q: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law concerning human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude, and, in connection therewith, creating new law expanding human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude to include knowingly trading anything of monetary value to buy or sell sexual activity with a minor and increasing the penalty to be life in prison without parole or release?
measures.s:
Proposition 133 proposes amending the Colorado statutes to:
mandate a sentence of life in prison without parole for child sex trafficking convictions; and
expand child sex trafficking to include buying sexual activity with a minor.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.

measures.no: A “no” vote on Proposition 133 keeps the existing felony criminal penalties for child sex trafficking with a sentencing range of 8 to 48 years in prison plus a mandatory parole period.
measures.f:
State Spending
The measure increases future state spending in the Colorado Department of Corrections (CDOC). Costs for the measure are estimated to begin in about 14 years. Initial costs are estimated at $180,000 in budget year 2041-42, and grow by that amount for several years thereafter. This would be an increase of $360,000 in budget year 2042-43, $540,000 in budget year 2043-44, and so on. These costs are not adjusted for inflation. Eventually, the increase will stabilize as the costs of new offenders staying longer are offset by a decrease in costs from life sentences ending due to an offender dying or potentially receiving a commutation or pardon.
The cost increase results from persons convicted of child sex trafficking serving a life sentence instead of a fixed term. It takes years for the first affected offenders to reach the point in their original sentence where they would have been paroled under current law, and that is when the added cost starts. This cost estimate reflects current sentencing data and values for state-run prison beds; actual costs will likely be higher in the future due to inflation, and if more individuals are convicted of child sex trafficking than under current law. Notably, costs for medical care will grow separately as offenders age in prison.
In addition, workload in the trial courts and agencies that provide representation to indigent offenders in the Judicial Department will minimally increase as cases with enhanced penalties generally take longer to process than cases with lesser penalties.
The measure does not specify a funding source to pay for the increased spending in the CDOC and it is assumed that these costs will be paid from the state General Fund. While the measure may reduce money available for other uses (the three largest of which are Health Care Policy and Financing, Education, and Higher Education), the likely effect of the measure on other programs is unknown and will depend on future budgeting decisions by the state legislature.

measures.t: Male and Female Participation in School and Collegiate Sports
measures.q: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law restricting participation in all K-12 and collegiate school sports based on the participant’s sex as determined by certain aspects of their biological reproductive system, and, in connection therewith, requiring a school, institution of higher education, or athletic association to designate each school or intramural athletic team or sport as male, female, or coeducational; only allowing participants to compete on the team or sport of their designated sex or to compete on a coeducational team; creating an exception to allow a female to participate on a male-designated team or sport if there is no female team available; prohibiting a government entity, licensing or accrediting organization, or athletic association from entertaining a complaint, opening an investigation, or taking other adverse action against a school for maintaining separate teams or sports for females; and providing the commissioner of education with the authority to enforce the proposed initiative for K-12 school districts?
measures.s:
Proposition 134 proposes amending the Colorado statutes to:
require that all elementary through collegiate school-based athletic teams and sports be designated as male-only or female-only based on biological sex, unless the team or sport is designated as open to participation by individuals of any sex or gender;
require schools and school districts to implement policies to ensure that students are assigned to gender-designated teams that align with their biological sex; and
prohibit investigations of, or penalties for, a school that designates a team or sport as female-only.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Proposition 134 means that all school-based athletic teams and sports must be designated as being for biological males or biological females only, or as mixed, and requires schools and school districts to adopt policies on sex eligibility for sports.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Proposition 134 means that individual schools, school districts, and athletic associations may continue to set their own policies in alignment with current state and federal law about who is eligible to participate on a team or in a sport.
measures.f:
State Spending
Proposition 134 will increase workload and legal costs by an indeterminate amount in the Colorado Department of Education if a school district is intentionally out of compliance with the measure and the Commissioner of Education is required to take remedial action. Legal services are provided by the Department of Law.
In addition, state institutions of higher education will have increased costs to adopt or update policies for interscholastic or intramural athletic programs to align with the requirements in the measure. Any costs are assumed to be paid by institutional revenue, such as tuition, fees, or athletic department revenue.
Local Government Spending
Proposition 134 will increase workload and may increase costs for schools, school districts and charter schools that offer interscholastic or intramural athletic programs to update and implement their policies. These costs are expected to be minimal. To the extent the Colorado Department of Education takes remedial action for noncompliance, legal and other costs may also increase for school districts.

measures.t: Prohibit Surgery on Minors in Response to Perception of Sex or Gender
measures.q: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes modifying existing law by prohibiting surgery on a minor for the purpose of altering the minor’s biological sex characteristics, and, in connection therewith, prohibiting any health-care professional or other person from knowingly performing, prescribing, administering, or providing any surgery to a minor for the purpose of altering the minor’s biological sex characteristics and prohibiting the use of state or federal funds, Medicaid reimbursement, or insurance coverage to pay for this type of surgery?
measures.s:
Proposition 135 proposes amending the Colorado statutes to:
prohibit surgeries on minors that alter their biological sex characteristics as a treatment in response to a minor’s perception of sex or gender, with certain exceptions; and
prohibit the use of state or federal funds or insurance coverage to pay for these surgeries.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Proposition 135 prohibits surgeries on minors that would alter their biological sex characteristics as a treatment in response to a minor’s perception of sex or gender, and prohibits the use of government funds or health insurance to pay for the surgeries.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Proposition 135 maintains Colorado law, which protects access to surgery altering minors’ biological sex characteristics and allows public and private health insurance programs to pay for these surgeries.
measures.f:
State and Local Government Spending
Proposition 135 will minimally increase workload and costs for the Department of Regulatory Agencies, which regulates health care professionals and insurers, to update rules and materials pertaining to gender- and sex-based surgeries and to handle complaints if prohibited surgeries are performed or paid for. Similarly, various state and local government agencies that employ health care professionals, such as the Department of Human Services and county hospitals, among others, will have additional workload to update their policies to ensure that their employees follow the measure. Legal costs may also increase for the state and local governments to respond to any allegations of noncompliance. Assuming health care professionals, insurance companies, and government agencies comply with the measure, any impact on state and local spending is expected to be minimal.
Proposition 135 may also slightly decrease state spending on health programs and employee health insurance from no longer paying for certain surgeries for minors related to gender perception. Specifically, to the extent the state Medicaid program covers these surgeries for minors, spending will decrease. Similarly, if private insurance companies no longer cover these surgeries, it may minimally contribute to lower health insurance premiums for state and local governments. Overall, any savings are expected to be minimal.

measures.t: Direct Sporting Goods Sales Tax Revenue for Conservation
measures.q: Shall there be a change to the Colorado Revised Statutes creating new law to increase water and land conservation funding without raising taxes, and, in connection therewith, through a voter-approved revenue change, allowing the state to keep and spend a portion of revenue from the state sales tax on sporting goods and equipment to conserve and protect Colorado’s water, land, and forests, prevent wildfires, support outdoor recreation training and activities, and reduce revenue spent on these conservation purposes if necessary to preserve funding for certain tax credits?
measures.s:
Proposition 137 proposes amending the Colorado statutes to:
direct a portion of existing sales tax revenues from purchases and rentals of sporting goods to be used for certain conservation, wildfire risk mitigation, and outdoor recreation programs; and
exempt that money from the state’s constitutional revenue limit, reducing the amount of money collected above the limit that is returned to taxpayers.
measures.sb: Legislative Council Staff, the nonpartisan research staff of the General Assembly: the opening of its analysis in the State Ballot Information Booklet (the Blue Book), mailed to every registered voter household. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.y: A “yes” vote on Proposition 137 directs existing sales tax revenue collected from sales of sporting goods to be spent on certain conservation, wildfire risk mitigation, and outdoor recreation programs, and exempts it from state revenue limitations.
measures.no: A “no” vote on Proposition 137 keeps the sales tax revenue collected from sporting goods in the state’s general budget and subject to the state’s revenue limit, with the revenue either spent on priorities decided annually by the legislature or refunded to taxpayers when required.
measures.f:
The measure transfers an estimated $175.0 million in the 2027-28 budget year, and increasing amounts in later years, from the state General Fund to pay for various programs related to forest restoration, wildfire mitigation, conservation, and outdoor recreation. It reduces TABOR refunds in years when revenue exceeds the TABOR limit.
State Revenue
The measure transfers an estimated $175.0 million in the 2027-28 budget year and $180.2 million in 2028-29 and future budget years for use on specified programs. This money would otherwise be available for the general state budget or refunded to taxpayers. The transferred revenue is divided between programs within GOCO (47.5 percent), Colorado State Forest Service and the Department of Natural Resources (47.5 percent), Colorado Parks and Wildlife (2.5 percent), and the Office of Economic Development and International Trade (2.5 percent).
The amount transferred may be reduced in years where the transfer would result in the reduction of certain income tax credits for families.
State Spending
The measure increases state spending by up to an estimated $175.0 million in budget year 2027-28 and $180.2 million in budget year 2028-29, and by increasing amounts in future years assuming sporting goods sales growth. Some funds may not necessarily be spent in the year they were received. Potential spending under the measure is shown in Table 1.
In years where state revenue collections are below the TABOR limit, the measure will reduce state money available for other uses (the three largest of which are health care, education, and human services); however, the exact effect of the measure on other programs will depend on budgeting decisions by the state legislature. In years where state revenue collections are above the TABOR limit, the measure has no impact on other state spending, but has impacts to taxpayers as described below.
Taxpayer Impacts
The measure will decrease the amount refunded to taxpayers in years when state revenue is over the TABOR limit. Based on forecasts from June 2026, the measure is expected to decrease refunds by $175.0 million in tax year 2027. Refunds in tax year 2028 are outside the forecast window. The impact on taxpayers depend on how this money would be refunded. The measure is expected to eliminate six-tier sales tax TABOR refunds in at least the 2027-28 budget year, by between $26 and $83 per single filer and between $52 and $166 per joint filer, with the actual amount dependent on income level.
Interactions with Other Measures
Proposition NN allows the state to keep and spend revenue that would otherwise be refunded to taxpayers under TABOR, up to a newly established limit. Because Proposition 137 reduces revenue subject to the constitutional revenue limit, Proposition 137 will reduce the amount of money the state actually keeps and spends under Proposition NN, if both measures pass.

qmoney.rule: Each committee's figures are added up from the Secretary of State's yearly files of money received and spent, for 2025 and 2026. A committee's side is read only from the purpose it registered. Some committees are not counted: one whose purpose names a measure only by its petition number, and small issue and political committees whose purpose does not name the measure. The files do not tie money others spent to a measure. So the real amounts for and against a measure may be higher than the figures here.

n.t: Fourteen statewide questions are on the November 3, 2026 ballot: seven amendments (81 to 87) and seven propositions (NN and 132 to 137). Thirteen were placed by citizen initiative and one, Proposition NN, by the state legislature. The words here are taken from the Blue Book that Legislative Council Staff mails to every registered voter household. The Secretary of State's own list of the measures also names each measure's issue committees and their registered agents; that page is linked, not copied.

Colorado keeps no statewide list of local ballot questions. The local questions shown here come from eight county clerks' own papers, read on October 16, 2026: the sample ballots of Douglas, Adams, Arapahoe, Larimer and Boulder counties, the ballot pages of Jefferson County and Denver, and El Paso County's TABOR notice. Front Range Passenger Rail District Ballot Issue 7A is shown from the Blue Book's notice. A question voted on in more than one county is shown once, for each county it reaches. The other counties are not read yet.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Colorado Secretary of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election and the June 30 primary, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, county offices are elected on party lines; cities, towns and other districts are nonpartisan. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists

Primaries. Where more people ran in a primary (June 30) than it could send on, everyone on that primary ballot is shown, with who went on to November, read from the general election list. Vote counts are the official results where they are loaded; where they are not, the race says so.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Colorado Secretary of State, each named among these sources; where something on a county’s ballot could not be shown, that county’s page says what and why.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the U.S. Census Bureau, the Regional Transportation District, the Colorado General Assembly and the Colorado Secretary of State: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For statewide offices, the Legislature, judges, county offices, mayors and city councils a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Candidates for soil and water, hospital and other small district boards and city clerks and treasurers show what they filed and, if they listed one, their campaign website. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: the official precinct results, added up here by county and district on the lines in force at that election; the results read here give no figures for a city or town, and the page says so there. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from your precinct, where the map files place it, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

Minnesota now has every local contest of 2020, 2022 and 2024: judges, county offices, cities, townships, school boards, soil and water and hospital districts, and local questions, read from the Secretary of State's own result files (as kept by the Internet Archive after the count was certified) and checked precinct by precinct against the certified results.
Precinct by precinct: on the Past results page, open any county's or contest's precinct table to see each precinct's figures, for the 44 states that publish them. They load only when you open them.

changelog.title: Past results for every state, and the ballot in Spanish (a draft)
items: Past results now cover 49 states and the District of Columbia: the November general elections of 2020, 2022 and 2024, from President down to county offices, cities, townships, school boards, special districts and ballot questions wherever the state or county publishes official figures. Wisconsin's official files are not reachable yet, and the page says so.

Figures are shown by county and by city or town. Where a state's figures come from a compilation rather than its own official count, they are labelled secondary and no winner is marked from them. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.
Each race page's "This seat before" now finds past elections in every loaded state.

On the draft site only: the ballot pages, menus, Help and the reading settings can be read in Spanish ("¿Leer en español?"). Each translated page says it was translated by Claude, an AI model, and not yet reviewed by a person. Names, office titles as printed and the words on your ballot stay in English; office titles show a Spanish translation beside the official English.
Ballot pages now say in one plain sentence what each office does, at the Beginner and Easy levels, with the official sources one tap away.

changelog.title: Past results: how places and seats voted in 2020, 2022 and 2024
items: New in Election Night: "Past results". Pick a state and a year (the November general elections of 2024, 2022 and 2020), then any contest on that ballot: names and parties as printed, votes and shares, the certified total and where it comes from, a county map, and the figures for each county, city or township.

North Dakota and Iowa are here in full, down to county offices, townships, soil and water districts and every ballot question. Illinois has Congress, the Legislature, judges and the statewide questions; Minnesota has President, Congress, the Legislature, Governor and the statewide offices. Their county and local races are next, and the page says which parts are still missing.

On The Ballot: race pages now have "This seat before", the same seat's past elections, with a note when the district's lines were different then. Ballot question pages have "Questions voters here decided before".
Every figure comes from the state's or county's official certified count and was checked against the official totals. Where two official records disagree, both are shown and nothing is changed.

changelog.title: The dashboard
items: New: a dashboard of the whole record, in three views. "Your place at a glance" shows any state or the whole country: what is on its ballot, who holds its seats, its ballot questions, and a link to its mail-voting facts. "The record, filtered" turns Congress's bills and floor votes into a sentence and charts you can narrow by chamber, topic and year. "Every state, side by side" puts all the states on one map, one measure at a time, with a two-state comparison.

Every figure is counted from the site's records when the page is built, and every chart says where its numbers come from and what they cannot tell you. Places can be compared; people are never ranked.
Beginner shows a few plain tiles; Medium adds the charts; Advanced opens the sources. Each view has its own address and a Share button.
The dashboard is linked from the home page, the menus, the On The Ballot door and Help.

changelog.title: Vote by mail, and questions answered
items: Every state's ballot page now has "Vote by mail or absentee": the last day to ask for a mail ballot and the last day to send it back for November 3, how to ask (the state's own link), how to send it back, what the envelope needs, how to track it, early voting in person, and what the state says for students at school elsewhere in the state or in another state, and for military and overseas voters. Every fact links to the state's own page or law and shows when it was checked. When a deadline has passed, the page says so and points to voting early or on Election Day.
"Your ballot" now says, under the election date, when to ask for a mail ballot.
The Congress ballot pages link each state to its mail-voting facts.

New: On The Ballot's questions page, with plain answers on voting by mail, students, military and overseas voters, moving, checking your registration, finding your polling place, when polls close, early voting, ID, tracking your ballot and a spoiled or lost ballot. Pick your state and each answer uses its own rules.
Every fact comes from the state's own election office or law, or from federal voting sites, and a second check re-read each source. The state election office always has the final word.

changelog.title: Share anything
items: Every part of the site now has a Share button: pages, races, ballot questions, counties, members, bills, votes, maps, the district lenses and Election Night. On a phone it opens your phone's own share sheet. On a computer it offers Copy link, e-mail, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Reddit (and text messages on a phone).
Nothing is sent until you pick a place. The place you pick then sees the link. No sharing buttons from those companies are loaded on these pages.
Every race, ballot question and county, down to the local contests, now has its own preview picture, so a shared link shows what it is about.
"Share my ballot" shares your precinct's ballot, after a note saying the link shows roughly where you vote. A shared link never carries your exact location.
The ready-made message sticks to the facts, for example: "U.S. Senate, Minnesota: who is on the November 3 ballot, from the official list."

_retention.t: In a retention vote the judge has no opponent: you vote yes or no on keeping the judge. The yes share needed differs by state, such as 60 percent in Illinois and 57 percent in New Mexico.
s: Frequently Asked Questions About Retention, Alaska Judicial Council
2026 retention recommendations, New Mexico Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission
Illinois Constitution, Article VI, Section 12 (Election and retention), Illinois General Assembly

x.es: En un voto de retención, el juez no tiene contrincante: usted vota sí o no a que el juez continúe en el cargo. La proporción de votos por el sí que se necesita varía según el estado; por ejemplo, 60 por ciento en Illinois y 57 por ciento en Nuevo México.

attorney_general.t: The attorney general is the state's top lawyer. The office speaks for the state in court, advises state agencies and enforces consumer laws.
s: About Our Office, Minnesota Attorney General
About the Office of Attorney General, Arizona Attorney General

x.es: El procurador general es el principal abogado del estado. La oficina representa al estado ante los tribunales, asesora a las agencias estatales y hace cumplir las leyes de protección al consumidor.

coroner.t: The coroner looks into deaths that are sudden, violent or unexplained to find the cause. In those cases the coroner signs the death certificate.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: El forense investiga las muertes repentinas, violentas o sin explicación para encontrar la causa. En esos casos, el forense firma el certificado de defunción.

council.t: The city or town council makes the city's laws. It also passes the budget and sets taxes and fees.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El concejo de la ciudad o del pueblo hace las leyes de la ciudad. También aprueba el presupuesto y fija los impuestos y las tarifas.

county_assessor.t: The county assessor sets the value of homes, land and other property for property taxes. The assessor does not set the tax rate.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
Ohio Revised Code 5713.01, County auditor as assessor
County Offices / Appraisal and Assessment Records, Alabama Department of Revenue

x.es: El tasador del condado fija el valor de las casas, los terrenos y otras propiedades para los impuestos sobre la propiedad. El tasador no fija la tasa de impuestos.

county_clerk.t: The county clerk keeps the county's official records. In some states the clerk also records deeds, issues licenses, runs elections and keeps court or board records.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
Texas Constitution, Article 5 (Judicial Department), Texas Legislature

x.es: El secretario del condado guarda los registros oficiales del condado. En algunos estados, el secretario también registra escrituras, emite licencias, administra las elecciones y lleva los registros del tribunal o de la junta.

county_commissioner.t: The county's governing board passes the budget, sets taxes and oversees services like roads. Its members are called commissioners, and in some places supervisors or police jurors.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-11, Board of County Commissioners, North Dakota Legislative Branch
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: La junta de gobierno del condado aprueba el presupuesto, fija los impuestos y supervisa servicios como los caminos. Sus miembros se llaman comisionados y, en algunos lugares, supervisores o jurados de policía.

county_court.t: County courts differ by state. New York's mostly hear crimes outside New York City; in Florida, Colorado and Nebraska they hear minor crimes, traffic and small lawsuits.
s: The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State
Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch

x.es: Los tribunales de condado varían según el estado. Los de Nueva York atienden sobre todo delitos fuera de la ciudad de Nueva York; en Florida, Colorado y Nebraska atienden delitos menores, casos de tránsito y demandas pequeñas.

county_surveyor.t: The county surveyor makes official land surveys and marks property lines and corners. The surveyor does this when a court or a landowner asks.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: El agrimensor del condado hace mediciones oficiales de terrenos y marca los límites y las esquinas de las propiedades. El agrimensor lo hace cuando un tribunal o un propietario lo pide.

county_treasurer.t: The county treasurer collects property taxes and keeps the county's money safe. The office shares it with schools, cities and other districts, but does not set how much is owed.
s: North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-14, County Treasurer, North Dakota Legislative Branch
Minnesota Statutes chapter 385, County Treasurer, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes

x.es: El tesorero del condado cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad y guarda de forma segura el dinero del condado. La oficina lo reparte entre escuelas, ciudades y otros distritos, pero no decide cuánto se debe.

court_of_appeals.t: The court of appeals is the middle level of state courts. Its judges check trial court rulings for legal mistakes when one side appeals, and they do not hold new trials.
s: Florida's Court Structure (Annual Report 2018-19), Florida State Courts
How courts work, California Courts Self-Help Center
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice

x.es: El tribunal de apelaciones es el nivel intermedio de los tribunales del estado. Cuando una de las partes apela, sus jueces revisan si las decisiones de los tribunales de primera instancia tienen errores legales, y no celebran juicios nuevos.

district_court.t: In most of these states the district court is the main trial court, where most cases start. In Alabama, Michigan, Washington, New York and a few other states it is a lower court for minor crimes, traffic and small lawsuits.
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch
Jefferson County District Court (Alabama Code 12-12-30 and following), Alabama Unified Judicial System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Michigan Compiled Laws 600.8301 (district court jurisdiction), Michigan Legislature
North Carolina General Statutes 7A-272 (jurisdiction of district court), North Carolina General Assembly
Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Washington State Courts
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State

x.es: En la mayoría de estos estados, el tribunal de distrito es el principal tribunal de primera instancia, donde empiezan la mayoría de los casos. En Alabama, Michigan, Washington, Nueva York y algunos otros estados, es un tribunal inferior para delitos menores, casos de tránsito y demandas pequeñas.

governor.t: The governor is the state's top leader. The governor signs or vetoes new laws, names many state officials and leads the state's military forces.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article V (Executive Branch), Michigan Legislature

x.es: El gobernador es el líder principal del estado. El gobernador firma o veta las nuevas leyes, nombra a muchos funcionarios estatales y dirige las fuerzas militares del estado.

juvenile_court.t: A juvenile court hears cases about children. These include young people charged with breaking the law and children who may be harmed or neglected.
s: State and Local Government, Chapter 1 Part B: The Judicial Branch, Louisiana House of Representatives
Guide to the Courts, Utah State Courts
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch
County Court, Nebraska Judicial Branch (separate juvenile courts in Douglas, Lancaster and Sarpy counties)

x.es: Un tribunal de menores atiende casos sobre niños. Estos incluyen a jóvenes acusados de violar la ley y a niños que pueden haber sufrido daño o descuido.

mayor.t: The mayor is the city's elected leader and, in some cities, runs city departments. Where the council hires a city manager, the mayor leads the council and the manager does the daily work.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El alcalde es el líder elegido de la ciudad y, en algunas ciudades, dirige los departamentos municipales. Donde el concejo contrata a un administrador municipal, el alcalde dirige el concejo y el administrador hace el trabajo diario.

probate_court.t: A probate court handles wills and the estates of people who have died, and often guardianships. In New York the judge is the Surrogate, and the court also handles adoptions.
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State
Michigan Compiled Laws 700.1302 (probate court jurisdiction), Michigan Legislature
Colorado Courts At A Glance, Colorado Judicial Branch

x.es: Un tribunal de sucesiones se encarga de los testamentos y de los bienes de las personas fallecidas y, a menudo, de las tutelas. En Nueva York, el juez lleva el título de Surrogate, y el tribunal también se encarga de las adopciones.

secretary_of_state.t: In most states, the secretary of state runs elections and keeps records, such as business filings. Other duties differ by state.
s: Secretary of State Divisions & Programs, Nebraska Secretary of State

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el secretario de estado administra las elecciones y guarda registros, como los documentos que presentan las empresas. Las demás funciones varían según el estado.

sheriff.t: In most states the sheriff is the county's top law officer. The office keeps the peace, runs the jail and carries out court orders; in Kentucky it also collects property taxes.
s: Minnesota Statutes 387.03, Powers, duties, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Minnesota Statutes 387.11, County jail, Minnesota Revisor of Statutes
Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el alguacil es el principal agente de la ley del condado. La oficina mantiene la paz, dirige la cárcel y cumple las órdenes de los tribunales; en Kentucky, también cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad.

state_board_of_education.t: The state board of education sets rules for public schools across the state. These cover what students should learn, what they need to graduate, and in Texas, textbooks too.
s: SBOE Homepage, Texas State Board of Education
State Board, Kansas State Department of Education
Texas Education Code, Chapter 7 (State Board of Education powers and duties), Texas Legislature
Texas Education Code, Chapter 31 (instructional materials), Texas Legislature

x.es: La junta estatal de educación fija reglas para las escuelas públicas de todo el estado. Estas reglas abarcan lo que los estudiantes deben aprender, lo que necesitan para graduarse y, en Texas, también los libros de texto.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

x.es: La Cámara de Representantes del estado (llamada Asamblea o Cámara de Delegados en algunos estados) es la cámara más grande. Sus miembros redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_treasurer.t: The state treasurer keeps the state's money safe. The office takes in and invests state money, pays it out, and in many states returns lost money to its owners.
s: Illinois Constitution, Article V, Section 18 (Treasurer - duties), Illinois General Assembly

x.es: El tesorero estatal guarda de forma segura el dinero del estado. La oficina recibe e invierte el dinero del estado, hace los pagos y, en muchos estados, devuelve el dinero perdido a sus dueños.

supreme_court.t: The state supreme court is the state's highest court. It hears appeals from lower courts and has the final say on state law (Texas also has a top court for criminal cases).
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
About the Courts, Kentucky Court of Justice
Judicial System Structure, Supreme Court of Ohio

x.es: La corte suprema del estado es el tribunal más alto del estado. Atiende apelaciones de los tribunales inferiores y tiene la última palabra sobre la ley estatal (Texas también tiene un tribunal máximo para los casos penales).

transit_board.t: These board members run a public bus and train agency, like Denver's RTD or Omaha's Metro. They set its rules and budget and hire its manager.
s: Board of Directors, Regional Transportation District (Denver)
Board of Directors, Metro Transit (Regional Metropolitan Transit Authority of Omaha)

x.es: Estos miembros de la junta dirigen una agencia pública de autobuses y trenes, como el RTD de Denver o Metro de Omaha. Fijan sus reglas y su presupuesto, y contratan a su gerente.

university_board.t: These elected boards run a state university. They guide the school, control how it spends its money and choose its president.
s: Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article VIII, Section 5, Michigan Legislature
Laws of the Regents, Article 2: The Regents of the University of Colorado

x.es: Estas juntas elegidas dirigen una universidad estatal. Orientan a la institución, controlan cómo gasta su dinero y eligen a su presidente.
